artifact_scope.value: Requirements, architectural, structural, behavioral, analytical, simulation, verification/validation, digital-twin, and lifecycle-management models and related diagrams are within scope.

citations.quote: Received: 29 November 2024 / Revised: 17 April 2025 / Accepted: 18 April 2025 / Published online: 21 May 2025 © The Author(s) 2025

The study conducted a systematic review with a bibliometric analysis to examine the extent of utilization and effectiveness of model-based systems engineering (MBSE) and concurrent engineering (CE) in managing and optimizing system design factors in complex systems across various domains, including space, healthcare, as well as active and assisted living and smart environments.
Research and development projects in various stages of technological maturity
Implementation of MBSE and CE principles in the development of complex systems
Improved efficiency, collaboration and quality in the design and development of complex systems through better architecture, requirements, specifications, lower costs, and time

This paper conducted a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis of the use of MBSE methodologies in complex engineering projects, with the scope of answering the question "Are MBSE and CE methodologies efficient during the early stages of the lifecycle of complex SoI's, optimizing system design factors and helping to minimize risks when compared to traditional engineering and/or design practices?".

Searches were performed in four scientific databases: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), United States National Library of Medicine (NLM), Scopus, and Web of Science (WoS), using a query formula adapted to the search engine syntax of each individual database.
Table 2 Identification of publications in databases

The steps of using the Rayyan platform were: importing libraries using RIS file extensions to transfer metadata about scientific publications between multiple platforms and software applications; extraction of RIS files from databases, or construction using the Zotero application (Takats et al. 2024), an open-source reference management software designed to help researchers collect, organize, cite, and share research materials; evaluation of each article by at least two evaluators; resolution of conflicts in special consensus sessions between evaluators; use of a waiting time of 2 weeks for requested access of publicly unavailable items.

According to the inclusion/exclusion criteria, the publications were evaluated as follows: 1. Inclusion of in extenso publications only in English (11 articles were excluded). 2. Exclusion of duplicate articles from searches in different databases (237 articles were excluded). 3. Exclusion of articles in which the titles and/or abstracts are not relevant to the previously formulated question (443 articles were excluded). 4. Exclusion of articles that could not be accessed in full (for 29 articles requests for full text were sent, only 2 articles were provided by the authors). 5. Exclusion of extenso articles that were not relevant to the previously formulated question (72 articles were excluded). 6. Inclusion of external sources known by the authors independent of the database searches (8 articles were included).

A structured quality appraisal process was applied to the selected studies to ensure methodological rigor and consistency. For this purpose, a standardized scoring framework designed for non-empirical data evaluation was used, namely the "Quality Scoring for Non-Empirical Studies" rubric developed by Laws and Winnard (2019).

The framework assigns a score ranging from 1 to 11 and consists of two parts, a hierarchical classification of evidence types (maximum 7 points) and a series of criteria assessing the rigor and clarity of the article (maximum 4 points).

The second part consists of four binary criteria (0 or 1 point each), which respectively evaluate whether the study possesses authenticity, transparently explains its methodology, clearly presents the information, and faithfully represents the cited sources. The scoring was performed independently by two reviewers, with the final quality score calculated as a mean of their total scores.

Data extraction was carried out by two reviewers. For situations where there were conflicting items, a special session was organized in which the reviewers participated together with a team leader for the parties to reach a

consensus. Data extraction can be seen in the Appendix section, Table 7, and the columns of the table refer to the following criteria: A. concurrent methodology; B. technological solution—the way in which the methodology was technically implemented; C. the purpose of using the methodology—based on the need to use the specified technology and the degree of complexity of the model used; D. population—technological maturity levels represented as TRL (technology readiness level); E. application type and general characteristics; F. the benefits of using the concurrent methodology; G. quality scoring—score obtained by completing the questionnaire "Quality scoring nonempirical data".

To perform the bibliometric analysis, the software VOSviewer version 1.6.20 (Van Eck and Waltman 2010) was used on Windows 11 Pro Operating System (OS). Additionally, to extract and add metadata to the articles collection and to export it as RIS file, the software Zotero version 6.0.36 was used on the same OS.

MBSE involves the use of comprehensive models to support system requirements, design, analysis, verification, and validation activities throughout the system's lifecycle. MBSE was identified as a primary methodology in approximatively 88% of the articles.

CE improves development speed primarily by promoting parallelization of activities, real-time collaboration, and early integration of multi-disciplinary perspectives. Unlike traditional sequential approaches, EC organizes design efforts within structured environments—such as CDFs—where domain experts co-develop system elements simultaneously, enabling immediate feedback and early conflict resolution.

In the implementation process, systems engineers define the requirements, structure, behavior, and validation criteria of the system within these tools using the Systems Modeling Language (SysML) in 50% of the articles.

OPM, on the other hand, provides a more holistic approach by creating combined object-process diagrams that illustrate both the structure and behavior of systems in a single unified model. OPM was only used in five articles (6%) (Sharon and Dori 2012; Ramos et al. 2013; Mordecai and Dori 2017; Menshenin and Crawley 2019; Kohen and Dori 2021).

The analyzed articles revealed that in fields such as healthcare, industrial systems, aerospace, and assistive technologies, where systems are highly complex and require precise coordination among various subsystems and teams, these methodologies can lead to a better handling of the challenges encountered.

In aerospace, found in 16% of articles (Bandecchi et al. 2000; McVittie et al. 2012; Bhasin et al. 2013; Haveman and Bonnema 2013; Sindiy et al. 2013; Hennig et al. 2015; Fischer et al. 2018; Menshenin and Crawley 2019; Cohen et al. 2022; Fuchs et al. 2022; Huang et al. 2022; Brusa et al. 2023; Bussemaker et al. 2020), SysML allowed for the detailed modeling of spacecraft systems
The populations addressed in the reviewed studies encompass various sectors and technology readiness levels (TRLs).

The focus on early and mid-development stages indicates that MBSE methodologies are predominantly utilized during the conceptualization and development phases of projects, benefiting from MBSE's ability to integrate various domain-specific inputs, providing detailed modeling capabilities, and facilitating collaboration among diverse teams.

In the 81 articles analyzed in this study, there were a total of seven methodological benefits identified that were common among many of the findings (see Table 3). Efficiency gains were identified in 37 articles (45.7%) ,representing articles that directly claimed improved total project efficiency, fewer design iterations needed to arrive at the final solution, and/or increased resource utilization efficiency. Increased collaboration potential was identified in 30 of the articles (37.0%)

Traceability was listed as a benefit in 13 articles (16.0%) , defined as the ability to associate engineering requirements to stakeholder needs in a useful manner. Error reduction was listed as a benefit in 13 articles (16.0%) , representing a decrease in error frequency during the design phase compared to traditional engineering methodologies, usually leading to a smaller required number of design iterations at the early project stages. Time reduction was claimed in eight articles (9.9%)

Finally, flexibility was mentioned in five articles (6.2%) , described as the ability to quickly adapt to change and to swiftly tailor specific methodological procedures to unexpected challenges as needed.
Co-occurrence analysis was performed to create keyword maps based on bibliographic data with full counting method setting.
According to the scoring rubric (see Table 6), 17.3% of articles (14/81) were assessed to be of poor quality (score of 6.5 or below).
A total of 44.4% (36) were determined to be of high methodological quality, defined as having a quality score of 9.5 or higher.

The primary findings of the systematic review presented in the second paper, Huang et al. (2022), demonstrate the successful application of MBSE using the Magic Grid framework to enhance the modeling and real-time simulation of satellite systems.

By using the SysML, the authors were able to create detailed models of the satellite's power subsystem, covering aspects such as demand analysis, behavior design, and constraint analysis. The implementation of real-time simulation monitoring verified the effectiveness and traceability of the modeling process
Notably, CE and MBSE appear in two different clusters, indicating that despite their relationship, they occupy distinct conceptual and functional spaces in the literature.

The separation suggests that these two paradigms are often discussed independently, reflecting the current state of the literature in which CE and MBSE are applied in complementary but siloed ways—CE as a managerial approach and MBSE as a technical implementation mechanism.

Throughout the study, a noted strength is the fact that the research evidence was selected and evaluated in different stages by multiple reviewers (i.e., more than 2 reviewers in selection and data extraction phase)

Limitations are related to the fact that the selected research evidences were not experimentally tested and had a lack of quantitative data or instruments designed to assess the actual inclusion impact in the systematic review.

Another limitation is the fact that 27 items (4.25% of the articles) could not be retrieved. The authors considered two articles (1 conference paper and 1 journal paper) as duplicates during the screening stage, determining the text to be very similar and including only the single journal paper Menshenin and Crawley (2019).

A characteristic that made it difficult to develop the study is the relatively wide range of articles found due to the database search being performed without time restrictions and in a broad array of fields.

Considering that no SysML and OPM combined solution has yet been universally accepted due to a lack of seamless integration of principles and tools, a future direction of this paper would consist of a study analyzing cases in which the two languages have been attempted to be combined

The findings of the study indicate that MBSE approaches consistently improve project outcomes by increasing efficiency, facilitating effective collaboration between different engineering disciplines, and reducing risks due to error, project time frame, and traceability issues.
The result of the study includes a comprehensive system model for the satellite power subsystem, verified and enhanced through real-time simulation.
